questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: As a student of history, Berlin is an awesome place to be. The international vibes in the city helps any foreigner feel welcome, while still exploring some German culture and history. I chose Berlin because I have an affinity for Germany, but I was unsure if i would be able to speak the language well enough to function in other places in the country. I now realise that I could have done so, but Berlin is especially good for english speakers.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: For anybody living in close proximity to Berlin, such as students in Copenhagen, it is awesome to be in a new place with a new adventure, whilst still feeling close to home.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Humboldt Uni were supremely efficient in helping me through email correspondence. Once i arrived, our Erasmuskoordinator arranged for all Erasmus Students of history to meet, where we were given all the required information, and were able to make some new friends.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus coordinator of Humboldt's history department arranged a meet-up, and afterwards, we could write to him or come to his office whenever needed. He was very helpful all throughout the semester, a super great, friendly and approachable guy.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: At the faculty of history atleast, Humboldt University has the best possible assistance to international students.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: If possible, look for your own housing in Berlin. More often than not, Humboldt will find you an accomodation in Adlershof Campus, which is very far away if you have to study in Mitte, for instance.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I found housing in Prenzlauer Berg, a very nice and central part of Berlin, but i know all will not be so lucky. Anything inside the Berlin Ringbahn is really ideal, look at WGgesucht and other places. I found my housing through a facebook group, and it turned out great, but one should always be very careful doing this.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
To register, one must first send application documents back and fourth from Humboldt, before arriving in the country. Because Germany's semesters are from october-marts and april-august, this paperwork will often not fit in with the automated time-schedules proposed in your own university's Erasmus application.
Once you're accepted, and you arrive in Germany, you recieve a letter in your physical mailbox (In Germany, everything is done on paper and not online). You take this letter to the Humboldt Administration (in their very limited office hours), and they then register you, you recieve your online account, your student-ID, etc..
For classes, you must then register the ones you want on this online account that you can now access, before the semester begins.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
Basically you just follow the instructions in their emails and letters. Mostly, you ask fellow students for advice, although i'm sure you could write an email to the administration and ask for advice as well. 
For registering classes, links to guide-videoes were send out per email. If there was any questions, the erasmus coordinator was very helpful and knowledgeable.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was 100% succesful in registering for the exact classes i wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: In Germany, you have to decide if you wanna do an exam for each class yourself. These exams then give additional ECTS points. This is worth considering from the beginning, as it must be written on your online learning agreement, and the teachers of the individual courses will want to know before long.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The history courses at Humboldt varies greatly in difficulty and quality. As with any university, it really depends on the individual professors. I will say, however, that taking courses in German, you really atleast have to understand the language. Most professors will have mercy on your speaking abilities, but you must be able to understand what they're saying to you.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style is mostly the same. In Vorlesungen, you sit and listen, in other courses, you debate throughout the lecture. It really is almost the same as in Denmark

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
DaF Deutsch Kurs (vor dem Wintersemester) - language course that prepares you for speaking and understanding German, costs a bit of money and takes a month, but i can only recommend it.
History of the communist secret police in Eastern Europe - very interesting course on Stasi and other opressive police forces during the could war.
Diplomatie und Spionage in der Frühen Neuzeit - super good master-level course on espionage and diplomacy between the years 1600-1900 .
Bachelorseminare neuere und neueste Geschichte, Markt und Koorporation: Geschichte der Europäischen Integration - Amazing course on european integration from the end of ww2 and forwards. Dr. Alexander Nützenadel is a great professor.
Deutschland und Frankreich seit dem Zweiten Weltkrieg, Konflikt und Verflechtung - very good Vorlesung for understanding the history behind the current relationship between Germany and France

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely look into the DaF studievorbereitend language courses, which they ask you if you want to apply for very early in the application process at Humboldt. They cost some money, but you get 4 hours of German training a day for a whole month, nothing prepares you better for your time at Humboldt. And, you get to meet people in similar situations to yourself, which is a great opportunity for making friends.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There were really no unexpected costs, aside from the very good language course at Humboldt. You pay 180 euroes for a "semester fee", but this gives access to all public transport in Berlin for the entire duration of the semester, so it is well worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food, drinks, and everything for living is less expensive than other places in Germany, and even Denmark. Over-expensive food or restaurants are priced like the danish ones.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Great opportunities for fun at Humboldt, if one wishes to engage in it. For instance, you can sign up for sport classes of all kinds.
Otherwise, living at a campus will give great social possibilites. Living in housing you found yourself, you will have to make friends locally and through classes and activities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely go to the first activities and meet--ups hosted by the university, they are paramount for forming good bonds for the entire semester.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go clubbing in Berlin, but go and embrace history and culture as well. They have 3 opera houses in Berlin, all very cheap for students. Go see historic sites, and remember to take some trips outside of the city aswell.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy to adjust to the culture, because they are a  lot like Danes in northern Germany.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: German students are hard to talk to, it is easier to speak with other international students. But, they are very kind, and if you manage to make some German friends, you will see that they are awesome.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing, Berlin was very welcoming as a whole.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciate the Berliners' fashion sense, because danish style is unbelieveably boring and unrecognisable. Also they have great beer.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't worry, you will have an awesome time here. German bureaucracy is no joke, there is a lot of physical paperwork involved, but it is all worth it. See it as a challenge, and remember that the Germans themselves meme on it. Because the semesters are in a weird time-frame compared to Denmark, you will have a lot of bureaucracy issues with the online erasmus-application. Don't worry, just communicate it and it will be no problem.
2. Be very proactive with seeking housing, it can become a nightmare if you don't have it taken care off. Get it done, so you can enjoy the time here.
3. Don't be put off by rumors of Berlin as a city, especially if you're not very good at German, or you don't like clubbing. Berlin is very welcoming, you don't have to speak perfect German, and you don't have to center your time here around clubbing. Berlin is a cultural hub, there is a whole crowd for jazz-clubs, classical music, sports, art, etc.. whatever you're into, you'll find it here.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: For Humboldt University, do the studievorbereitend language courses, even if you have to save up a bit of money for them! And remember to consider which courses you wanna do exams in as well.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I have found myself 10x more capable than i thought through this experience. 1. day in my apartment i locked myself out, and had to call 8 German locksmiths before one of them understood my broken German, and came to help. The Erasmus-experience is packed full of challenges, but you grow 10x as a person in comparison to a normal semester at home. And if you like foreign cultures, languages and history, an exchange trip is an absolute must. You will feel alive every day.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest  challenges were the language barriers and struggling to keep up with people who speak the language as their first language. This, along with the bureaucracy found in Germany, made the experience difficult, but it is absolutely worth it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you've had the idea to go on an exchange semester, and you kinda wanna do it but you're not really sure - stop thinking and just go! Academically, professionally and personally, this is what gives you an adventure of a lifetime, and it will set you apart. Just go!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
